The adjective postmortem means "occurring after death" or "relating to something done or examined after death." When you place this word in front of a noun, it tells you that whatever that noun refers to — a report, an examination, a discovery — happened after a person or creature had already died.

The clearest and most classic example is the phrase postmortem examination. This is the medical procedure (also known as an autopsy) in which a doctor carefully inspects a dead body to find out the cause of death, the manner of death, or any hidden medical conditions. The examination cannot happen while the person is alive — by definition, it happens after death. That "after death" quality is exactly what the adjective postmortem is pointing to.
How It Works as an Adjective

As an adjective, postmortem always comes before a noun and modifies it. It answers the question: "When did this happen, or what period does this belong to?" The answer is always: after death.

Here are some phrases where it naturally appears in its literal, medical/legal sense:

  • Postmortem examination — the inspection of a body after death
  • Postmortem report — a written document that records what a doctor found during that examination
  • Postmortem interval — the amount of time that has passed between the moment of death and the moment the body is discovered or examined (used heavily in forensic science)
  • Postmortem changes — the physical changes a body undergoes after death (skin color change, stiffening of muscles, decomposition, etc.)
  • Postmortem lividity — the bluish-purple discoloration that appears on the skin where blood has pooled due to gravity, after the heart has stopped pumping
  • Postmortem findings — the things discovered and observed upon examining a dead body

In all of these, the word is doing one precise job: marking that something belongs to the period or process that follows death.
Shades and Nuances of the Literal Meaning

Even within its literal sense, the adjective captures a few related but distinct ideas:

1. Happening after death in time
Something that occurs simply because the person is now dead. For example, postmortem changes in the body begin immediately after the heart stops. These changes — like rigor mortis (stiffening of muscles) or decomposition — are described as postmortem because they are caused by or occur during the state of being dead.

2. Done after death for the purpose of understanding death
A postmortem examination or postmortem report is not just happening after death in time — it is specifically performed after death with the goal of understanding what happened. This is a deliberate human action taken in response to death.

The adjective covers both shades. Context usually makes clear which one is meant.

Over time, the word postmortem escaped the world of medicine and entered everyday language as a figurative adjective. Here, it no longer refers to a literal death — instead, it refers to the end of any event, process, or endeavor, treating that ending as if it were a death.

In this figurative sense, postmortem means: "occurring after the conclusion of something, typically involving a careful analysis of what went wrong or what happened."

Think of it this way: just as a doctor examines a dead body to understand what caused death, people figuratively "examine" a failed project, a lost game, a collapsed deal, or any concluded event to understand what caused its failure or shaped its outcome.

Examples:

  • Postmortem analysis — a careful review of a project, campaign, or event after it has ended, asking: "What went wrong? What went right? What can we learn?"
  • Postmortem meeting — a meeting held after a project fails (or even after it succeeds) to discuss what happened and extract lessons
  • Postmortem discussion — a conversation about an event after it is over and can no longer be changed
  • Postmortem review — a structured evaluation after the conclusion of something

You might hear this in business ("The team held a postmortem review after the product launch flopped"), in sports ("The coach conducted a postmortem analysis of the season"), in technology and software engineering (teams regularly schedule postmortem meetings after a system crash or failed release), and in politics or journalism ("Analysts began a postmortem examination of why the party lost the election").

Whether used literally or figuratively, the adjective postmortem always carries the same underlying logic:

Something has ended — permanently, irreversibly. What follows now belongs to the "postmortem" phase: the phase of looking back, examining, and understanding.

The literal use says: this person's life is over; we are now in the phase of examining what that ending means.

The figurative use says: this event or effort is over; we are now in the phase of examining what that ending means.

In both cases, the adjective marks a specific moment in time — the after — and assigns everything that happens in that after to its domain.
A Key Nuance: It Is Always Retrospective

One subtle but important quality of postmortem as an adjective is that it is inherently retrospective — it looks backward. You cannot plan a postmortem before the event ends. You can plan for one, but the postmortem analysis itself only becomes possible once the thing being analyzed is fully over.

This means the word also carries a quiet sense of finality. When something is described as requiring a postmortem examination (literal or figurative), it is acknowledging that what's done is done — there is no reversing it, no going back. The only thing left is to understand it.

To sharpen your understanding: compare postmortem with the word preliminary (meaning "before the main event"). These two sit on opposite ends of a timeline.

  • Preliminary examination → happens before the main event or conclusion
  • Postmortem examination → happens after death or conclusion

This contrast helps anchor the adjective clearly: it is firmly and always in the after.

Postmortem (adjective) = describing something that occurs or is done after death (literal sense) or after the end of an event or endeavor (figurative sense), usually with the purpose of examining, analyzing, or understanding what happened. It always implies finality — whatever is being examined is completely over — and it always looks backward in time.
